items.title: [ScienceDaily] Low testosterone linked to 18% higher risk of dying from cancer
items.content_html: A major international study tracking more than 26,000 men found that very low testosterone levels were associated with an 18% higher risk of dying from cancer later in life. Surprisingly, testosterone itself showed no clear link to prostate cancer, although two other sex hormones did. Researchers believe low testosterone could be an important early warning sign of future health risks, particularly when levels fall below 8.6 nmol/L.

items.title: [medicalxpress.com] Novo Nordisk heart drug cuts inflammation but fails to reduce cardiovascular events
items.content_html: Novo Nordisk’s experimental drug ziltivekimab lowered inflammation markers but did not reduce major cardiovascular events in the phase 3 ZEUS trial of 6,376 adults with atherosclerotic disease, chronic kidney disease and inflammation. Over a median follow-up of 33 months, the primary outcome occurred in 17.6% of people receiving the drug and 17.7% receiving placebo. Researchers presented the full results Nov. 7 at the American Heart Association’s scientific sessions and published them in the New England Journal of Medicine. Novo Nordisk halted the related HERMES and ATHENA trials after a monitoring committee judged them unlikely to succeed; its ARTEMIS trial is continuing, with results expected in the first half of 2027.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Avoid these 5 common open enrollment pitfalls
items.content_html:
Whether you’re among the 53.5% of Americans who get their health insurance through work, the 20.1% enrolled in Medicare, or the 10.5% purchasing ACA coverage, mid-October or early November typically marks the start of the open enrollment period for next year’s insurance coverage.

Life would be easier if your health insurance coverage stayed the same if you liked it or adapted to your life automatically if you didn’t. Unfortunately, we mere mortals have to make decisions about our upcoming healthcare plan each year, in part because employers and other providers make regular changes to their insurance offerings—in addition to any legal changes that might affect federal benefits and ACA coverage.

The good news is that employers, Medicare providers, and the ACA marketplace typically time their open enrollment period to coincide, giving you November to make decisions about next year’s benefits.

But just because you know when to expect open enrollment season—who can miss all the open enrollment carols on the radio?—doesn’t mean you’re prepared for the important decisions you need to make. In fact, there are several common mistakes that could cost you big bucks in 2027 if you don’t know how to avoid them.

Here’s what you need to know about the most common open enrollment pitfalls.

The pitfall: missing a deadline

We all know how fast the fourth quarter tends to go. One minute you’re passing out candy to adorable Spidermen/Gwens and the next you’re eating Christmas cookies while making resolutions for 2027. The open enrollment deadline can get lost in the holiday shuffle.

For reference, these are the important deadlines for enrolling in a health insurance program during open enrollment:

  • ACA Marketplace has two enrollment deadlines:
    • December 15, 2026 for coverage beginning January 1, 2027
    • January 15, 2027 for coverage beginning February 1, 2027
  • Medicare: Enroll by December 7, 2026; coverage changes take effect January 1, 2027
  • Employer-sponsored health insurance coverage: Your deadline will vary depending on your employer. Your HR department will have the necessary information.

There are two possible problems you may face after missing an open enrollment deadline:

  1. You might have to go without insurance. If you miss the ACA open enrollment period, you can’t get insurance through the health insurance marketplace this year—unless you qualify for a special enrollment period. To qualify, you’d need to have gotten married or divorced, had a baby, moved, or lost your previous healthcare coverage.
  2. You might be reenrolled in the same plan. Medicare beneficiaries who miss the open enrollment deadline are typically reenrolled in the same plan if it’s still offered. But it may not be the best option for your needs.

Workers with employer-sponsored insurance plans may still be able to enroll after missing a deadline, depending on how draconian the HR department is—but it’s not a good idea to count on it.

The pitfall: procrastination

As busy as this time of year can be, it’s rare that we miss an open enrollment deadline because it slips our minds. Instead, it’s much more likely that we procrastinate until the last minute. Humans tend to put off decision-making that feels overwhelming, confusing, or deeply boring—which is precisely the kind of choices you need to make during open enrollment.

Luckily, we know how to beat procrastination. If you know you have open enrollment decisions to make but have been putting them off, follow these steps to keep from procrastinating yourself sick:

  1. Make it an appointment on your calendar. Set a specific time to deal with open enrollment paperwork. Schedule it in your calendar the same way you would a work meeting or doctor’s appointment.
  2. Gather necessary information beforehand. After you make your “open enrollment appointment” on your calendar, generate a list of the things you think you’ll need to make decisions. Start gathering this information a little at a time. Some of the data you might need includes the names, birthdates, and Social Security numbers of every member of your household, pay stubs or tax returns to show your household income, how much you paid out of pocket in 2026, and your preferred healthcare providers and medications.
  3. Spend no more than an hour on open enrollment. The reason we avoid tasks like open enrollment is that our brains convince us they’ll take forever. So give yourself permission to work for only 60 minutes. Stop at the end of the hour, even if you’re not completely done. Just schedule the next appointment before you quit for the day.
  4. Don’t let perfectionism thwart your decisions: Part of what makes open enrollment nerve-racking is the fact that it’s impossible to know ahead of time if you’ve made the best decisions for next year’s healthcare needs. Trying to find the perfect plan option that will maximize your healthcare coverage while minimizing your out-of-pocket costs can drive you nuts, since a year of robust health may follow a year of multiple ER visits. Instead of aiming for a perfect plan, base your decision on what’s probable for 2027.

The pitfall: making assumptions

We often try to reduce the complexity of tough decisions by making assumptions. Unfortunately, open enrollment is not a time when assumptions are your friends. It’s very common for healthcare plans to change their coverage and options from one year to the next, even when the plan itself keeps the same name or offered coverage level.

Here are some of the common changes that could catch you flat-footed if you’re not looking for them:

  • A revised formulary: Your plan may no longer cover the medication you’ve been taking for years—or it may start covering a medication that you’ve previously had to pay for out-of-pocket.
  • Increased annual deductible: Next year, you may have to pay more out of pocket before your coverage kicks in.
  • Revised coinsurance amount: Coinsurance is the percentage of the cost of a covered service that you’re responsible for paying, after meeting the annual deductible. Don’t assume that the coinsurance amount will stay the same from year to year.
  • Increased premium amounts for dependents: The monthly premium required to cover your spouse and children can often go up from one year to the next.
  • Increased out-of-pocket maximum: The maximum amount you might pay during 2027 may be higher than the limit set for 2026.

The pitfall: choosing based on price

Expecting a current plan will stay the same is not the only way assumptions could steer you wrong. It’s also easy to make assumptions about how well a plan will fit you based on cost.

For example, rather than compare options one by one, you might decide to enroll in the most expensive plan, assuming the higher cost means it’s better coverage. But the best health insurance plan for your needs depends on your specific situation. Springing for the high-premium/higher-coverage plan may be a waste of money for a marathon runner who sees the doctor only for an annual checkup. (Unless they tear an ACL, of course . . .)

But you might make a similar mistake in the other direction by signing up for the plan with the lowest premiums. It’s easy to assume lower monthly premiums will cost you less overall if you don’t consider the other costs you’ll have to pay. But lower premiums typically means lower coverage levels.

This price catch-22 can contribute to your procrastination, since it may feel like you’re going to overpay no matter what. (As a cynical veteran of open enrollment, I can honestly say that feeling is correct. You are probably going to pay more than you could have if you’d had a crystal ball.)

However, there are some questions you can ask yourself to help reduce the likelihood of making a decision-by-price mistake during open enrollment:

  1. Did my 2026 plan cover my healthcare needs? This gives you a baseline for determining if a new plan will suit your situation.
  2. How much did I spend out of pocket this year? If you spent more than you expected or more than you budgeted for, that can help you identify where you need more robust coverage.
  3. What confused me about my current coverage? Now’s an excellent time to clear up that confusion by contacting your HR representative, the ACA helpline at 1-800-318-2596, or Medicare at 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227).

The pitfall: not checking your work

A jaw-dropping 90% of employers have open enrollment errors. These errors may include relatively minor problems like billing mistakes, as well as more major issues like eligible employees not getting enrolled despite opting in—leaving them without coverage.

Before you turn in your enrollment paperwork (or, more likely, hit the SUBMIT button), go back through the entire process to double-check that all the information is correct. Then, when you receive the documents, read through them for accuracy, as well. It’s much easier to fix a clerical error during open enrollment than after the new plan year begins.

Set yourself up for a healthy 2027

Open enrollment may rival filing taxes for the worst annual adulting requirement—but taking some time to make well-thought-out decisions for next year’s health insurance plans will always be something you’re glad you did.

items.title: [lemonde.fr] US measles cases reach 5,182 as elimination status faces review
items.content_html: The United States has confirmed 5,182 measles cases in 2026, the highest annual total since 1991. State officials have reported at least eight related deaths, including deaths of young children. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the federal public health agency, has counted four deaths, leaving the national toll disputed. The case total is more than twice the 2,289 recorded in all of 2025. Officials and medical experts have linked the resurgence to falling vaccination coverage and distrust of health authorities. In the 2025-26 school year, 92.4% of kindergarteners received the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, down from 95.2% in 2019-20. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the World Health Organization’s regional body for the Americas, is due to review U.S. measles-elimination status next week. The review will consider whether the virus has again established sustained transmission. The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000.

items.title: [mdpi.com] Medical AI studies find gains uneven and clinician oversight essential
items.content_html: Artificial intelligence is spreading into clinical documentation, imaging, patient communication and hospital operations, but evidence that it improves care in routine settings remains uneven, a review published in the Journal of Clinical Medicine found. Trials of clinician-reviewed ambient documentation showed modest benefits that varied by product, while errors persisted. Many hysteroscopy studies assessed images retrospectively rather than patient-level outcomes, and reported operating-room scheduling gains largely came from simulations. A separate preprint found that clinicians’ everyday AI requests often differ from the tasks in medical AI benchmarks. A study of pancreatic cancer patients linked use of an AI assistant’s psychological-support feature to lower anxiety and better quality-of-life scores, while a survey study linked dependence on generative AI to weaker clinical reasoning. Researchers and clinicians stressed human review, local validation, privacy safeguards and training. The clinical-practice review recommends defining a need, measuring baseline performance and setting criteria for expanding or withdrawing AI systems.

items.title: [sciencefeatured.com] Higher BMI over time linked to faster cognitive decline in older adults
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A 24-year study of several thousand middle-aged and older Americans found that higher average body mass index (BMI) over time was associated with faster declines in memory and thinking. A team led by University of Georgia researcher Suhang Song reported the findings in the Journal of Neurology. The association was strongest when cognitive abilities were assessed about eight years after weight measurements and was more pronounced among participants who were older when the study began. The observational study cannot establish that higher weight causes cognitive decline or that weight loss would prevent it. The researchers noted that participants reported their own height and weight and that the analysis could not account for physical activity. The team called for further research into possible biological mechanisms and future interventions.

Because declining blood flow can occur years before Alzheimer's symptoms appear, the discovery raises hopes for preventing or delaying the disease before memory loss begins.

items.title: [Benjamin Cane] Microservices can work for low-latency workloads—if you design for it
items.content_html:
Microservices can work for low-latency workloads if you design them that way.

Over the years, many people have told me, “Microservices don’t work when you need low latency; use a monolith.” I get it; for many, this advice comes from negative experiences.

When you break a monolith into multiple services, you’re replacing function calls with network calls. Those network calls introduce latency, and the more services you depend on, the slower the overall request becomes.

But does that really mean microservices can’t be used for low-latency systems? No, and I say that from experience.

I’ve spent a lot of time working on low-latency distributed systems, and I think the key is designing your architecture to compensate for the added overhead.

Caveat: Low-latency is subjective; designing a system for single-digit milliseconds vs. double- or triple-digit milliseconds will differ, since every additional digit changes your tolerance.

Locality Matters

One thing I really like about cell-based architecture is that it encourages locality, and locality is good for latency. We often talk about cells in the context of resiliency. They contain failures, reduce the blast radius, and help keep one problem from impacting the entire platform.

But they also provide a pattern for keeping communication between services local.

Suppose you are building a microservices-based platform with four or five services that each request must pass through. If you spread those services across multiple availability zones, clusters, or regions, you'll create significant latency.

Depending on the network topology, that traffic may cross additional switches, routers, firewalls, and other infrastructure. Crossing regions also introduces significant physical distance, which adds even more latency.

flowchart TB Client[Client] subgraph R1[Region 1] direction TB A1[Service A] B1[Service B] C1[Service C] D1[Service D] A1 ~~~ B1 ~~~ D1 ~~~ C1 end subgraph R2[Region 2] direction TB A2[Service A] B2[Service B] C2[Service C] D2[Service D] A2 ~~~ B2 ~~~ D2 ~~~ C2 end Client --> A1 Client --> A2 A1 -->|1| B2 B2 -->|2| C1 A1 -->|3| C1 A1 -->|4| D2 D2 -->|5| C1 A2 --> B1 B1 --> C2 A2 --> C2 A2 --> D1 D1 --> C2

Now, let's imagine those same services running close together within the same Kubernetes cluster and availability zone.

Keeping those services local can significantly reduce the network infrastructure each request has to traverse. In the best case, the services might even be running on the same physical or virtual server.

flowchart TB Client[Client] subgraph R1["Region 1: local cell / one AZ"] A1[Service A] -->|1| B1[Service B] B1 -->|2| C1[Service C] A1 -->|3| C1 A1 -->|4| D1[Service D] D1 -->|5| C1 end subgraph R2["Region 2: separate cell / one AZ"] A2[Service A] -->|1| B2[Service B] B2 -->|2| C2[Service C] A2 -->|3| C2 A2 -->|4| D2[Service D] D2 -->|5| C2 end Client --> A1 Client --> A2

Of course, Kubernetes clusters can span multiple availability zones, so simply being in the same cluster doesn't necessarily guarantee locality. If you're optimizing purely for network latency, keeping communicating services within the same availability zone is generally preferable. But that doesn't mean your entire platform should depend on a single availability zone.

Multiple cells that each independently run in an availability zone is one option. Another option is to leverage locality-based routing. You can still design for multi-AZ resiliency while preferring local communication.

Applying a low-latency lens to cell-based architecture lets you deliberately optimize how services communicate within each cell.

But locality comes with trade-offs. You need to manage how traffic is distributed, ensure each environment has enough capacity, and think carefully about data consistency. All of this adds operational complexity.

If low latency is important enough, those trade-offs may be worth it.

Stop Rebuilding Connections

Another common source of unnecessary latency is frequent connections.

When two microservices communicate hundreds or thousands of times per second, closing and re-establishing a new connection for every request is highly inefficient.

Every new TCP connection requires a three-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, and ACK.

If you're using TLS, you've also got the additional negotiation required to establish a secure connection.

Each of these steps adds network round trips, and when you're trying to squeeze milliseconds out of a system, those costs matter.

sequenceDiagram participant Client participant Server Note over Client,Server: New connection per request loop Each request Note over Client,Server: TCP handshake
and optional TLS setup Client->>Server: Request Server-->>Client: Response Note over Client,Server: Close connection end

In contrast, a persistent connection allows you to establish a connection once and reuse it for multiple requests.

While this is absolutely possible with HTTP/1.1, protocols like HTTP/2 take this further by allowing multiple concurrent requests over the same connection.

Instead of constantly opening and closing connections, keeping a pool of reusable connections open and using them efficiently can significantly reduce request latency.

sequenceDiagram participant Client participant Server Note over Client,Server: Reuse an established connection Note over Client,Server: TCP handshake
and optional TLS setup
once loop Multiple requests on the same connection Client->>Server: Request Server-->>Client: Response end

But this performance improvement has a trade-off: load distribution.

Connection Reuse Requires Rethinking Load Distribution

Let’s imagine you’ve got ten instances of a service and your client microservice is configured to establish reusable connections based on what it needs.

With HTTP/2, your client might only need a single connection to handle a significant amount of traffic. But if that connection is pinned to one backend instance, all those requests would end up going to the same instance.

Meanwhile, the other nine instances are sitting idle.

flowchart LR P[Client] --> L[Layer 4 balancer] subgraph Backends[Backend instances] direction TB P1[Instance 1] P2["Instance 2
No requests from this client"] P3["Instance 3
No requests from this client"] end L ==>|One HTTP/2 connection
many requests| P1[Instance 1]

When clients frequently establish new connections, layer 4 (network-level) load balancers have more opportunities to distribute those connections across your microservice instances. But when clients reuse a small number of long-lived connections, those same load balancers have fewer opportunities to redistribute traffic. Balancing connections isn't necessarily the same as balancing requests.

There are multiple options to approach load-distribution with reusable connections, such as having clients open a pool of connections and round-robin sending traffic across that pool. You could also leverage something like a service mesh, which does this for you.

flowchart LR Q[Client] --> M[Request-aware proxy] M -->|Reused connection| Q1[Instance 1] M -->|Reused connection| Q2[Instance 2] M -->|Reused connection| Q3[Instance 3]

This is a lesson I learned the hard way: early on, when embracing HTTP/2 in a microservices platform, I was unpleasantly surprised to find two or three microservice instances being hammered with traffic while seven others sat idle. But once we fixed it (we used a service mesh), our latency suddenly dropped as we distributed traffic better, letting each microservice run with less stress.

It was a great lesson, I just wish I didn’t have to learn it the hard way…

Avoid Unnecessary Waiting

This is a topic of a recent talk I gave at P99 Conf 2026.

HTTP/1.1 supports persistent connections, but it doesn't support multiplexing independent requests over a single connection the way HTTP/2 does.

In practice, an HTTP/1.1 connection typically handles one request at a time. If your client has more requests than available connections, some requests have to wait for a connection to become available.

HTTP/2 changes that by allowing multiple requests to be in flight concurrently over the same connection. This can significantly reduce the time requests spend waiting for available connections.

While HTTP/2 clients make asynchronous communication feel synchronous, there are always trade-offs with asynchronous communication. Managing timeouts, knowing when it’s safe to retry, etc. All topics I covered in the talk.

Managing asynchronous communication introduces complexity, but when you're trying to squeeze every millisecond out of a system, that complexity can be worth it.

Final Thoughts

Microservices will always introduce some communication overhead compared to the internal function calls of a monolith. But that doesn't necessarily make them a bad choice for low-latency workloads.

When I talk to folks who prefer monoliths over microservices, many have had bad experiences because their platforms weren't designed for low latency.

Maybe their services communicated across regions unnecessarily, they weren't reusing connections efficiently, or their load distribution created hot spots.

It's easy to understand why a monolith might seem like a better option in those situations. To play devil's advocate, solving these problems introduces complexity.

Microservices aren't free, and not every organization needs the independent scaling, ownership boundaries, and operational flexibility they provide. For many organizations, though, those benefits are valuable enough to justify the additional complexity.

My advice for anyone building a low-latency platform is simple: don't immediately discount microservices.

You can absolutely build low-latency systems with microservices. You just have to design for it, and make sure the complexity is worth it.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] A discussion on women at work with Laëtitia Vitaud
items.content_html:
There’s never a “right” age for a woman at work. Early in their careers, women may face discrimination based on assumptions about whether they’ll take maternity leave. Later, they’re subject to a new set of age-based biases.

In this FC Live, Fast Company senior editor Jon Gluck led a conversation with Fast Company contributor and author Laëtitia Vitaud about the unique advantages that women of all ages bring to the workforce and what those advantages could mean for the future of work.

Despite the challenges women face throughout their careers, Vitaud argues that women are especially poised for the AI revolution because “their working lives have frequently included interruptions, pivots, reinventions, periods of part-time work, freelance activity, caregiving, and reentry into employment.”

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Jeff Bezos praised Raising Cane’s. Its founder built a $22 billion fortune by breaking 3 fast-food rules
items.content_html:
Raising Cane’s isn’t following the standard fast-food playbook.

From its limited menu to the employee dress code, founder Todd Graves is charting his own path in a competitive industry. Now, one of the world’s richest men is pointing to his chicken finger empire as a prime example of the power of entrepreneurship.

In a recent Fox News interview, Jeff Bezos pushed back on the notion that building a successful business and becoming a billionaire made someone a villain.

Instead, he pointed to entrepreneurs who expanded their companies and created thousands of jobs. For the Amazon founder, Graves is a prime example of that.

“There’s nothing wrong with making unbelievably good chicken that people love,” he said. “And it doesn’t make him a bad person.”

However, although Graves and Bezos are both billionaires, the former followed a different playbook than the latter.

In 1996, Graves, who was 24, opened the first Raising Cane’s in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. He used loans from friends, family, and the Small Business Administration, as well as savings from his jobs as a boilermaker and an Alaskan salmon fisherman.

Three decades later, the ethos of the fast-food chain remains the same: a simple menu centered on chicken fingers, fries, coleslaw, Texas toast, and Cane’s Sauce.

Even now, the smallest change, such as the addition of a sandwich combo, can create anxiety and stress.

“To tell you the truth, man, I kind of wish we didn’t even have it on the menu. It’s like 3 or 4 percent of sales. And it slows us down,” Graves previously told Inc. “I wish we didn’t have it, but I won’t take it away now.”

This small admission reflects the chicken chain’s broader philosophy. While Bezos launched a publicly traded giant, Graves has focused on keeping Raising Cane’s limited in scope and tightly controlled.

Keeping the company private

The biggest difference between the two billionaires may be their views on taking a company public.

Forbes estimates Graves currently owns about 92 percent of the company, with a net worth of approximately $22 billion. The founder has said Raising Cane’s has no plans to go public, a choice he has tied to preserving the chain’s culture.

A key executive has echoed the same sentiment. “We have no plans on that,” AJ Kumaran, the company’s co-CEO and COO, told Restaurant Business. “We are privately held because we want to remain that way.”

By comparison, Bezos took Amazon public just three years after its founding. It debuted on the stock market in May 1997 at $18 a share, raising $54 million to fuel its growth.

Focusing on employees

However, even though Graves is committed to retaining control of the business, he takes a more relaxed approach with his employees.

At Raising Cane’s, crew members wear casual uniforms and music has been allowed in the kitchen since the early days. It is a deliberately relaxed approach that stands apart from Amazon’s more regimented structure.

A commitment to charity

Yet, even amid their differing approaches to business, both Bezos and Graves are committed to charitable giving.

Bezos’s Earth Fund, backed by a $10 billion pledge, has distributed about $2.4 billion to date. His Day 1 Families Fund has donated more than $850 million to nonprofits addressing homelessness.

After the Texas floods in 2025, Graves donated $1 million to the Red Cross. In August, Graves told Dallas Weekly that the company had given more than $165 million to charitable causes over its first 30 years, something he hopes will continue.

Raising Cane’s didn’t immediately respond to a request from Inc. for comment.

—Amaya Nichole

This article originally appeared on Fast Company’s sister website, Inc.com.

items.title: [science.org] JWST image-processing method boosts exoplanet sensitivity up to 15-fold
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Astronomers have developed a physics-based method to remove residual starlight from James Webb Space Telescope images, improving sensitivity to faint planets by two to 15 times and revealing the known giant exoplanet 51 Eridani b at a wavelength where earlier processing failed. The method, called Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets, or FLIP, models the telescope’s optics and adjusts for small changes that make conventional reference-star images imperfect matches. The method works with existing observations without changes to telescope hardware. The team is now reprocessing the hundreds of coronagraphic images JWST has collected to look for additional planets. Researchers say the approach could ease strict stability requirements for future observatories, but further work is needed to reduce computing costs and test it on larger data sets.
